To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the default risk on British colonial loans was lower than on other loans and that the British colonial government was able to use its influence in London to obtain a better price for colonial bonds than for other bonds.

(1) the British Empire reduced the risk of default by its colonies; (2) the British Empire increased the risk of default for the metropolis; (3) the British Empire did not reduce the cost of borrowing for the colonies; (4) the British Empire raised the cost of borrowing by the metropolis; and (5) the British Empire was not an important factor in the spread of the Industrial Revolution to the colonies.
the default risk of British colonial governments was eliminated by the British government and that the British government did this in a way that reduced the cost of colonial borrowing.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (1) the measurement of the effects of institutions; (2) the measurement of colonial borrowing costs; (3) the measurement of default risk; (4) the measurement of empire; (5) the measurement of political subjection; (6) the measurement of economic consequences; and (7) the measurement of causality.
the measurement of the costs of borrowing, and the effects of the institutions of colonialism on those costs.
the financial and political consequences of colonial rule.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Empire was not a financial burden, but rather a financial asset to Britain, and that the financial consequences of the Empire were beneficial to the British people.
colonial borrowing was cheaper because of lower default risk, not because of any ‘colonial effect’.
the British empire was a great success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the British Empire was an effective financial instrument, but not a particularly efficient one.
the British Empire was a financial empire.
the British Empire was a financial success for the British, and that the costs of empire were not borne by the colonists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dummy variable approach is not appropriate to the study of the impact of empire on the terms of borrowing.
the effects of institutions are often not what they seem, and that we should not take them as given but try to understand them.
the use of dummy variables to measure institutions should be avoided unless the researcher is willing to explain the underlying mechanisms.
